pass_b_english: … is Lord; you alone are Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 83:18). He said “alone” because of the one Godhead. He called him Father of the age to come, though he is the Creator of the past ages as well, because it was from the time of the dispensation that he became widely known to men. So he called him Father of a created nature, not of an uncreated one; for the Father of the uncreated and consubstantial Son is one. And pointing to the immeasurable greatness of his Godhead, he said: “Of his peace there is no bound” (Isaiah 9:7).

Jeremiah too, or Baruch (for the two have one book), speaks of him in solemn words: “This is our God; no other shall be compared with him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterwards he was seen on earth and lived among men” (Baruch 3:35-37). If, then, it is not understood in a way worthy of God, that the passage before us was spoken so because both the ineffable hypostases have the same Godhead, it remains to fall into godlessness and say that the God and Father who begot him is not our God and is not to be compared with his Son.

So the argument of those who slander God the Word as lesser and a subordinate has fallen and vanished altogether. For how could another be beyond compare with God, he “with whom no other shall be compared”? And again: “Let the gods who did not make the heaven and the earth perish from the earth. The Lord, who made the heavens by understanding, he is the living and true God” (Jeremiah 10:10-12). This is said because no other Godhead is true except that of the genuine Son of God, through whom and from whom the heavens too were brought forth, together with the whole world.

And Paul, the most eminent of men, keeping the same sequence as the prophets, gives the words that befit him. To Titus he writes: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:13-14). By declaring “of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ,” he shows that the Son does not stand second in substance, and that he is without beginning in relation to the great God the Father. Indeed, one can see it from what is plain on the surface: if the Son is small, how will the Father be great? If there “was a time when he was not” for God the Word, there was a time when the name of Father did not exist. May we be pardoned for daring to say such things; we say them because of the senselessness of others. “For reverence,” as they say, “is a fine habit for those who practise it.”

By saying “who gave himself for us, to purify for himself a people of his own,” and not “to purify a people for another,” he brings out something further, in keeping with what has been mentioned. For it signifies that he has received as his own the one Godhead, self-determining and good, the cause of all things. To die for one’s own handiwork, if one may put it so, belongs to a creator and not to a creature; and to acquire the people for himself belongs to a beloved Son whose Godhead and kingdom are no different from the Father’s.

Carrying the argument on, this great and true interpreter sets out to show that he is at once a loving and saving God, and at once that it was by prevailing upon himself, and not by yielding to a higher Godhead, that he came to be with us as one of us, without change and without sin. He says: “When indeed the kindness and love for mankind of God our Saviour appeared, not by works which we had done, but according to his great mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:4-5).

To the Colossians he both gives rebuke and lays the foundation of the very first theology concerning him, writing, as was said already in the chapter “On the Consubstantial”: “Why according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ Jesus? For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily” (Colossians 2:8-9), that is, in substance. For he is by nature fullness itself, being in his substance the Father’s Godhead. “For he did not count it robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2:6). But we, through his goodness, received grace from the fullness, a grace which by nature, as servants, we did not have. So John says: “And from his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace” (John 1:16); that is, the grace of rebirth in place of the grace we cast away when we set aside the first ordinance, given about the one tree. “For no longer,” …

choices.issue: Garbled clauses, a slogan given a Scripture reference, incomplete references, bracket filler
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English made 27.27 say the Son is 'Father as a creator and not of uncreated nature' (he is Father of a created nature); rendered τὸ ἀμέγεθες as 'something simple' (immeasurable greatness); made the Father 'the one who created' (ὁ τεκών: who begot); said the slanderers' argument had 'fallen away and spread' (vanished); turned 27.33 into 'as if there were another divinity that is not true'; turned ὑπεραποθανεῖν into 'not to surpass' (to die for); made the Word 'veil himself … through a change and through sin' (prevail upon himself … without change and sin); and turned καταβολή into 'disparagement' (foundation). It cited the Arian slogan 'there was when he was not' as John 1:1; the reference is removed. References: 'Titus 2:13' made Titus 2:13-14 (the quotation runs to 'zealous for good works'), 'Jeremiah 10:11' made Jeremiah 10:10-12, 'Baruch 3:35' made 3:35-37, 'Colossians 2:9' made 2:8-9; Isaiah 9:7 and Titus 3:4-5 added. Bracket [the distinction] removed.
